source_text: Στιχ. ιη΄. Τοῦ δὲ Ἰησοῦ ἡ γέννησις οὕτως ἦν. . . . . . . . (1–2) Ὧδε μὲν γεννήσεως μέμνηται ὁ εὐαγγελιστὴς, κατʼ ἀρχὰς δὲ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου, τῆς γενέσεως. Ἐνταῦθα μὲν γὰρ λέγει· Τοῦ δὲ Ἰησοῦ λριστοῦ ἡ γέννησις οὕτως ἦν, ἐκεῖ δὲ, Βίβλος γενέσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. Τίς οὖν ἡ διαφορὰ τῆς γεννήσεως καὶ τῆς γενέσεως; καὶ ὡς ἀμφότερα ἐπὶ Χριστοῦ λαμβάνεται; Ὥσπερ ὁ λόγος οὗτος ὁ προφορικὸς κατὰ τὴν οἰκείαν φύσιν ἀναφής ἐστι καὶ ἀόρατος· ὅταν δὲ ἐν βιβλίῳ γραφῇ, καὶ οἱονεὶ σωματωθῇ, τότε καὶ ὁρᾶται καὶ ψηλαφᾶται· οὕτως καὶ ὁ ἄσαρκος τοῦ Θεοῦ Λόγος καὶ ἀσώματος, οὕτε ὁρώμενος, οὕτε γραφόμενος κατὰ τὴν θεότητα, ἐπειδὴ ἐσαρκώθη, καὶ ὁρᾶται καὶ γράφεται. Διὰ τοῦτο, ὡς σαρκωθέντος, καὶ βίβλος ἐστὶ τῆς αὐτοῦ γενέσεως. Ἀλλʼ οὐκ ἐξήτηται ἐνθάδε τὸ, διὰ τί εἶπε βίβλος, καὶ οὐκ εἶπεν ὅρασις (3), ἢ λόγος· ἀλλὰ τὸ, τί ἐστι γέννησις, καὶ τί γένεσις; Διαφέρει γένεσις καὶ γέννησις. Γένεσις μὲν γάρ ἐστι παρὰ Θεοῦ πρώτη πλάσις γέννησις δὲ ἡ ἐκ καταδίκης τοῦ θανάτου διὰ τὴν παράβασιν ἐξ ἀλλήλων διαδοχή. Καὶ ἔτι, ἡ μὲν γένεσις τὸ ἄφθαρτον ἔχει (4) καὶ ἀναμάρτητον· ἡ δὲ γέννησις τὸ παθητὸν καὶ ἁμαρτητικόν.
orientation: Origen is commenting on Matthew 1:18, where the evangelist says 'the birth of Jesus was thus,' and contrasts it with the opening phrase 'book of creation.'
pass_a_gloss: Verse 18. The birth of Jesus was thus. . . . . . . . (1–2) Here the evangelist mentions birth, but at the beginning of the Gospel, creation. For here he says: The birth of Jesus Christ was thus, but there, Book of creation of Jesus Christ. What then is the difference of birth and of creation? and how are both taken in the case of Christ? Just as this spoken word according to its own nature is intangible and invisible; but whenever it is written in a book, and as it were embodied, then it is both seen and touched; so also the fleshless Word of God and bodiless, neither being seen nor being written according to divinity, since he became flesh, is both seen and written. Because of this, as of one who became flesh, there is also a book of his creation. But it has not been sought here, why he said book, and did not say vision (3), or word; but what is birth, and what creation? Creation (genesis) differs and birth (gennesis). For creation is the first formation from God; birth is the succession from one another out of the penalty of death because of the transgression. And further, creation has the incorruptible (4) and sinless; birth has the passible and prone to sin.

pass_b_english: Verse 18: “Now the birth of Jesus took place in this way” (Matthew 1:18). Here the evangelist mentions “birth,” but at the beginning of the Gospel he mentions “creation.” For here he says, “Now the birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way,” while there he says, “The book of the creation of Jesus Christ” (Matthew 1:1). What, then, is the difference between “birth” and “creation,” and how are both applied to Christ?

Consider a spoken word. By its own nature it is intangible and invisible. But when it is written in a book and, so to speak, given a body, then it is both seen and touched. The same is true of the Word of God. Before he became flesh he was fleshless and bodiless, neither seen nor written according to his divinity. But because he became flesh, he is both seen and inscribed. For this reason, since he became flesh, there is also a book of his creation.

But the question here is not why he said “book” and not “vision” or “word.” The question is what “birth” is and what “creation” is. Creation and birth differ. Creation is the first formation by God. Birth is the succession of one generation from another that comes from the penalty of death because of transgression. And further, creation possesses what is incorruptible and sinless, while birth possesses what is passible and prone to sin.
